page-privacy-online-meta-description: Practical steps and privacy-preserving apps for protecting your personal information online: private browsers, encrypted messaging, device settings, and data deletion requests.
page-privacy-online-title: How to protect your privacy online
page-privacy-online-hero-description: Practical, easy steps and privacy-preserving apps to protect your personal information online and take control of your digital life.
page-privacy-online-summary-item-1: Privacy-first browsers, encrypted messaging, and email aliases keep your data from being collected as you browse.
page-privacy-online-summary-item-2: A few simple settings changes, like limiting location tracking or rejecting cookies, cut off invisible tracking at the source.
page-privacy-online-summary-item-3: Data brokers sell your personal information, but where the law gives you a right to opt out, you can get your records deleted without paying anyone.
page-privacy-online-summary-item-4: Privacy-preserving alternatives exist for nearly every app, from email to search, notes to maps, so protecting your data doesn't mean sacrificing convenience.
page-privacy-online-how-description-1: Anyone can make proactive choices online to protect personal information. Secure your digital footprints by using privacy-preserving software, adjusting device preferences, and submitting legal data deletion requests.
page-privacy-online-how-description-2: The strategies below are a starting place to protect your privacy online and mitigate tracking across standard web environments.
page-privacy-online-tools-description: You can protect your personal information online by switching from standard web tools to privacy-preserving alternatives built to collect less data.
page-privacy-online-tools-browser-first: The easiest place to start is your browser, and it is a change nobody else has to make with you. Roughly seven in ten people browse with Chrome and more than nine in ten searches go to Google, both built by an advertising company and designed for tracking.
page-privacy-online-tools-browser-callou: Same engine as Chrome with same look and feel. Bookmarks, passwords, and extensions carry straight over. Open source, blocks ads and trackers with no setup, and searches with Brave Search by default instead of Google.
page-privacy-online-tools-browser-tests: Being the most popular browser does not make Chrome the best one. On independent privacy testing it is among the weakest of the major browsers, and there are plenty of alternatives worth a look.
page-privacy-online-tools-browser-tests-: Compare all popular browsers at PrivacyTests.org
page-privacy-online-tools-search-descrip: Your search history is the most revealing log you generate: what you buy, who you look up, what symptoms you search for. Point your default at an engine that does not build a profile out of it, like Brave Search or DuckDuckGo.
page-privacy-online-tools-blocking-descr: Scripts that follow you between unrelated sites are what assemble a profile of your habits. Blocking them is automatic in Brave. On any other browser add uBlock Origin, and set the browser itself to block third-party cookies.
page-privacy-online-tools-messaging-desc: Ordinary SMS is readable by your carrier and by anyone who can compel them. End-to-end encrypted apps, like Signal, keep the contents between you and the person you are talking to. Not everyone has to switch at once: install one and you will usually find some contacts already there, and those conversations can move first.
page-privacy-online-tools-email-descript: Most free mailboxes are paid for by scanning what arrives in them. Providers like Proton Mail and Tuta encrypt your mail at rest, so the company holding it cannot read it, and both will import an existing inbox when you move.
page-privacy-online-tools-aliases-title: Give every service its own address
page-privacy-online-tools-aliases-descri: One address used everywhere is what lets data brokers and breach databases stitch your accounts into a single profile. Alias services, like SimpleLogin, hand each site a separate address you can switch off the moment it starts attracting spam.
page-privacy-online-tools-signin-title: Stop signing in with Google or Facebook
page-privacy-online-tools-signin-descrip: Every "Sign in with Google" button tells Google which services you use and when, and ties all of those accounts back to one identity. Sign up with an alias instead and let a password manager, like Bitwarden, fill the login in one click: the same convenience, and no shared identifier linking everywhere you have an account.
page-privacy-online-vpn-title: What a VPN can do, and what it cannot
page-privacy-online-vpn-alert-title: A VPN does not make you anonymous
page-privacy-online-vpn-alert-descriptio: It changes who can watch you. Your internet provider and the network you are on lose sight of where you are going, and the VPN company gains it. You are moving trust, not removing it.
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-lead: The distinction matters. A VPN genuinely solves some problems and does nothing at all about others, and the marketing rarely separates the two.
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-1-does: Hides which sites you visit from your internet provider and from the network you are on
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-1-not: Hide them from the VPN company, which now sees all of it instead
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-2-does: Replaces your IP address, so sites cannot place you by location or tie separate visits to one household
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-2-not: Make you anonymous to any site you sign in to
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-3-does: Protects you on networks you have no reason to trust, like public Wi-Fi
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-3-not: Add encryption that HTTPS is not already providing
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-4-does: Lets you appear to be somewhere else, which helps when a service is blocked where you are
page-privacy-online-vpn-table-4-not: Stop browser fingerprinting, cookies, or tracking tied to your accounts
page-privacy-online-vpn-trust: Because the operator sees everything your provider used to, its honesty is the entire product. That is why free VPNs are so often the worst offenders: running servers costs money, and when a subscription is not paying for them, your browsing is.
page-privacy-online-vpn-criteria-lead: Properly auditing a VPN is slow, expensive work, which is why very few earn a recommendation. What to look for:
page-privacy-online-vpn-criteria-1: Published ownership and jurisdiction, so you know who is actually holding your traffic and which government can ask them for it.
page-privacy-online-vpn-criteria-2: A no-logs claim an independent auditor has tested, rather than one asserted on a marketing page.
page-privacy-online-vpn-criteria-3: Signup that never asks who you are, and a way to pay that is not tied to your identity.
page-privacy-online-vpn-criteria-4: A track record: how the company behaved the last time it was subpoenaed, seized, or breached.
page-privacy-online-vpn-tor-description-: Tor can do some of what a paid VPN does, for free, with no company in the middle. Traffic is relayed through three volunteer-run nodes, and no single one of them knows both who you are and where you are going, so there is no operator holding a log to sell or to be forced to hand over.

Tor comes with honest trade-offs. It is slower, some sites block it outright, exit nodes can be run by anyone including governments, and sophisticated observers can still correlate traffic by timing. It is still a strong option for ordinary private browsing, but not for logging in or shopping: signing in tells the site who you are, and hostile exit nodes have been caught stripping HTTPS to steal what passes through.

Tor works better the more ordinary people use it. Every additional user makes the crowd larger and every individual in it harder to pick out, and that crowd is what protects the journalists, activists, and people escaping abuse who rely on it. Everyday browsing adds to it.
page-privacy-online-vpn-tor-learn-more: <link>How Tor works, and what it does not protect against</link>
page-privacy-online-vpn-relay-title: Apple Private Relay, a low-barrier option for millions
page-privacy-online-vpn-relay-descriptio: On Apple hardware, iCloud+ includes Private Relay, which sends Safari traffic through two separate relays so that neither Apple nor the site you are visiting can see both who you are and what you are loading. It covers Safari only, is an Apple service on Apple's terms, and it is no substitute for Tor if you are genuinely at risk. It is, however, a significant improvement over unprotected Chrome, is already sitting on hundreds of millions of devices, and switching it on takes one toggle.
page-privacy-online-settings-description: Secure software functions best when you update device and app settings to mitigate the sharing of location and background data with hardware manufacturers.
page-privacy-online-settings-gpc-descrip: GPC sends an automatic do-not-sell-or-share signal to every site you visit, and under California's CCPA and laws in states including Colorado and Connecticut it has to be honored. Brave and DuckDuckGo send it by default and Firefox can be set to. Chrome and Safari do not send it at all, so there it takes an extension.
page-privacy-online-settings-cookies-des: Websites use confusing layouts, so-called dark patterns, to make handing over everything the easy path. Take the extra moment to find "Reject All" or "Manage Preferences". Rejecting is not a paywall: the page still loads, and the site still works.
page-privacy-online-settings-devices-des: Review privacy menus on your smartphones, tablets, and computers. Turn off location tracking for apps that do not strictly require it and limit diagnostic data sharing with manufacturers.
page-privacy-online-settings-cookies-cli: A cookie consent banner being dismissed with "Reject all", after which the page loads normally.
Reject cookies by default. Declining typically takes one click, and the page loads exactly the same.
page-privacy-online-policies-description: Data brokers collect and sell personal information without asking. Many places now give you a legal right to see that data and demand its deletion, including the European Union and United Kingdom under the GDPR, a growing list of US states, Brazil, and Canada. What that right covers, and whether anyone will enforce it for you, varies enormously by country. Where you have it, using it is one way to start taking back control of your digital footprint.
page-privacy-online-policies-services: Paid removal services advertise heavily and perform worse than the advertising suggests. In Consumer Reports' testing, people filing opt-outs by hand had 70 percent of their records gone within a week, while the services managed between zero and 59 percent over the same period.<crStudy></crStudy> Consumer Reports and the Electronic Frontier Foundation both still point people at doing it themselves, and Privacy Guides will not list a removal service that is affiliated with the data broker industry, which rules out much of what you see advertised.<privacyGuidesRemovals></privacyGuidesRemovals>
page-privacy-online-policies-optout-desc: Hundreds of companies you have never heard of buy, package, and resell your address, your income, your health interests, and where your phone has been. Where the law gives you a right to deletion, they have to honor a request. The work is that you have to send one to each of them.
page-privacy-online-policies-registry-de: California residents can file one free request through <link>the state's DROP registry</link>. Every data broker registered there, more than six hundred of them, has to check it at least once every 45 days and delete what it holds on you. It is the only centralized free route of its kind anywhere.
page-privacy-online-policies-manual-desc: If you would rather not hand your details to another company to do this, go to the brokers' privacy policies yourself and file deletion requests through their "Consumer Privacy Rights" links. It is slow, and it is free.
page-privacy-online-apps-description: Day-to-day replacements for the tools most people already use, picked because they are built to collect as little about you as possible. Which of them matter depends on what you are protecting, and from whom.
page-privacy-online-apps-more: This is a sampling, not a full catalog. <privacyGuides>Privacy Guides</privacyGuides> maintains vetted recommendations with the reasoning behind every entry, and <awesomePrivacy>Awesome Privacy</awesomePrivacy> is a broader directory of privacy-respecting alternatives.
page-privacy-online-app-brave-descriptio: A Chrome-compatible browser that blocks ads and trackers by default, and switches your default search at the same time
page-privacy-online-app-firefox-descript: The last mainstream browser not built on Google's engine; set tracking protection to strict on first run
page-privacy-online-app-mullvad-browser-: Tor Browser's anti-fingerprinting work, built by the Tor Project for use without the Tor network
page-privacy-online-app-tor-browser-desc: Routes each request through three volunteer relays, so no single hop knows both who you are and where you went
page-privacy-online-app-duckduckgo-descr: Search without a profile: queries are not logged or tied back to you
page-privacy-online-app-brave-search-des: Results from an independent index rather than a resold one, with no query tracking
page-privacy-online-app-ublock-origin-de: Blocks ads and trackers outright, with no paid allowlist behind it
page-privacy-online-app-signal-descripti: The gold standard for encrypted messaging, run by a non-profit
page-privacy-online-app-simplex-descript: Messaging with no user identifiers at all, so there is no account to link a conversation back to
page-privacy-online-app-session-descript: No phone number and no central server: an account is just a random ID you share
page-privacy-online-app-proton-mail-desc: Swiss-hosted email your provider cannot read, with built-in address aliases
page-privacy-online-app-tuta-description: Encrypts the whole mailbox, including subject lines, contacts, and calendar
page-privacy-online-app-addy-description: Open-source, self-hostable email aliases, so every service gets an address that leads nowhere else
page-privacy-online-app-simplelogin-desc: Aliases you can switch off the moment one starts attracting spam, and keep your real address off sign-up forms
page-privacy-online-app-bitwarden-descri: A unique password for every account, synced across your devices and encrypted so the company cannot read it
page-privacy-online-app-mysudo-descripti: Bundles of throwaway identities, each with its own phone number, email address, and handle to hand out and retire
page-privacy-online-app-mullvad-vpn-desc: No email, no account, flat monthly price, and a no-logs claim that has survived repeated audits
page-privacy-online-app-proton-vpn-descr: An audited VPN with open-source clients and a genuinely usable free tier
page-privacy-online-app-quad9-descriptio: A Swiss non-profit resolver that blocks known malicious domains and keeps no logs; your lookups move from your provider to them
page-privacy-online-app-2fas-description: Open-source two-factor codes for iOS and Android, with backups you control instead of a vendor's cloud
page-privacy-online-app-cryptomator-desc: Encrypts your files before they reach the cloud you already use
page-privacy-online-app-notesnook-descri: End-to-end encrypted notes that stay unreadable to the people hosting them
page-privacy-online-app-organic-maps-des: Offline navigation on OpenStreetMap data, with no location tracking
page-privacy-online-app-grapheneos-descr: A hardened Android build for Pixel phones, with no Google services
page-privacy-online-app-tails-descriptio: A live system you boot from a USB stick: everything runs over Tor, and nothing is left on the machine at shutdown
page-privacy-online-app-f-droid-descript: A catalog of free software for Android, installed without tying every download to a Google account
page-privacy-online-resources-descriptio: Privacy online is not only a question of which apps you install. These organizations research surveillance, litigate against it, and teach people how to protect themselves.
page-privacy-online-resource-eff-descrip: Litigates and campaigns against surveillance, and publishes Surveillance Self-Defense, a set of how-tos organized around the threats you actually face.
page-privacy-online-resource-privacy-int: Investigates and challenges surveillance by governments and companies, with a focus on where it lands hardest outside wealthy countries.
page-privacy-online-resource-noyb-descri: Enforces European data-protection rights in court, which is much of the reason a deletion request has to be honored at all.
page-privacy-online-resource-tor-descrip: Builds and maintains the Tor network and Tor Browser, the free anonymity infrastructure that journalists, activists, and people escaping violence rely on.
page-privacy-online-resource-ludlow-desc: Research, education, and resources for privacy, autonomy, and dignity online, and the home of NBTV.
page-privacy-online-resource-web3privacy: An ecosystem of people, projects, and organizations advancing digital rights, with research, education, and app explorers.
page-privacy-online-resource-access-now: <link>Access Now</link>: digital rights worldwide, and a 24-hour digital security helpline.
page-privacy-online-resource-fpf: <link>Freedom of the Press Foundation</link>: source protection and digital security training for journalists.
page-privacy-online-resource-security-in: <link>Security in-a-Box</link>: Front Line Defenders' tools and tactics for activists and human rights defenders.
page-privacy-online-resource-prc: <link>Privacy Rights Clearinghouse</link>: consumer-facing tools and explainers on data rights in the United States.
page-privacy-online-resource-newsguild: <link>Digital Security for Journalists</link>: a resource collection from The NewsGuild of New York.
